faq.title: Frequently asked questions about the Northern Lights
faq.intro: Everything you need to know to chase the Northern Lights — from Kp values to what to wear at -25 °C.
faq.a.about1: The name RepoTracker comes from a Finnish belief that the Northern Lights are created when a magical fox, "Repo", strikes the snow with its tail, sending sparks into the sky.
faq.a.about2: Who is behind this project? RepoTracker is a solo project, designed and maintained by a single Northern Lights enthusiast. From coding the maps to tracking solar data — everything you see here is the result of one person's passion for the Northern Lights.
faq.a.about3: Because this is a one-person project, your feedback and support mean the world. Every coffee donated helps cover server costs and API fees that keep the real-time data running for everyone.
faq.q.when: When is the best time to see the Northern Lights?
faq.a.when: The Northern Lights are best seen on dark, clear nights in autumn and spring. The best time is usually between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m. In northern Finland, a Kp index of 3–4 is enough; in the south you usually need Kp 5–6 or higher.
faq.q.values: What do the values on the map mean?
faq.a.values: The Kp index describes geomagnetic activity. The higher the value, the more likely Northern Lights are visible:
faq.q.clouds: How does cloud cover affect visibility?
faq.a.clouds: Clouds block the Northern Lights completely. Always check the cloud cover before heading out — a clear sky is essential.
faq.q.dark: Do I need a dark place?
faq.a.dark1: Yes. Light pollution in cities reduces visibility significantly. Move away from street lights and choose an open area with a clear view of the northern horizon.
faq.a.dark2: It is still possible to see Northern Lights in towns like Rovaniemi — just step into a slightly darker spot and you have a good chance when the forecast is favorable.
faq.a.dark3: Tip: sometimes a phone camera picks up the Northern Lights before your eyes do.
faq.q.south: Can the Northern Lights be seen in southern Finland?
faq.a.south: Yes, but less frequently. A high Kp index (≥ 5–6) and clear skies are required.
faq.q.know: How do I know when the Northern Lights will appear?
faq.a.know: Use real-time tools like RepoTracker for live forecasts. You can also follow data from NOAA SWPC and the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
faq.q.bz: What are solar wind and IMF Bz?
faq.a.bz: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles from the Sun that delivers energy to Earth's magnetic field. The IMF Bz value indicates the orientation of the interplanetary magnetic field — a strong negative Bz greatly increases the chances of seeing the Northern Lights.
faq.q.gear: What should you keep in mind when going hunting for the Northern Lights?
faq.a.gear1: Dress warmly — one thick coat is not the best option. Several thin layers under a proper winter coat keep you warmer and give flexibility.
faq.a.gear2: Wear warm shoes and gloves, and bring extra clothes if you plan to be outside for a long time.
faq.a.gear3: If you are traveling by rental car, stay on plowed public roads. Do not drive on poorly maintained or unplowed forest roads — you can get stuck in the snow and help may take a long time to arrive in winter.
faq.a.gear4: If you head out on your own, respect private yards, military areas and any place where you are unsure whether entry is allowed.
faq.a.gear5: Tip: be careful where you stop the car. Bus stops are ideal. Avoid stopping on the road to prevent dangerous situations.
faq.a.tips1: Useful safety guidance for visitors to Lapland is available as a PDF from the Finnish rescue services.
faq.a.tips2: A few good Northern Lights-watching spots near Rovaniemi: Ounasvaara, Olkkajärvi parking lot near Apukka Resort, and Arktikum Park.

blog.title: Northern Lights articles & guides
blog.intro: In-depth reads to help you understand, chase and photograph the Northern Lights.
blog.post1.title: Northern Lights photography for beginners
blog.post1.excerpt: Camera settings, gear, and field tips to capture the Northern Lights — even with a basic DSLR or modern smartphone.
post1.pagetitle: Northern Lights Photography for Beginners — RepoTracker
post1.lead: You don't need a 5 000 € rig to bring home a stunning Northern Lights photo. Here is the practical setup that works for almost anyone.
post1.h2.gear: Gear: the minimum that actually works
post1.p.gear1: Any camera that lets you control shutter speed, ISO and aperture manually will work — entry-level mirrorless and DSLR bodies are perfect. The single most important accessory is a sturdy tripod. The Northern Lights move, but your camera must not.
post1.li.gear1: Lens: wide-angle (14–24 mm full-frame, 10–18 mm APS-C) with a fast aperture of f/2.8 or wider when possible.
post1.li.gear2: Tripod: stable, with a head that holds position in the cold.
post1.li.gear3: Remote or self-timer: avoids vibration when you press the shutter.
post1.li.gear4: Spare batteries: cold drains them fast — keep them in an inside pocket.
post1.p.settings1: Use these as a baseline, then adjust based on Northern Lights brightness and movement:
post1.li.set2: Aperture: as wide as your lens allows (f/2.8 or wider)
post1.li.set3: Shutter speed: 2–8 seconds. Faint Northern Lights → longer; fast-dancing Northern Lights → 1–3 s to freeze structure.
post1.li.set4: ISO: 1600–3200 to start. Push higher only if needed.
post1.li.set5: Focus: manual, set to infinity. Test on a bright star with magnified live view.
post1.li.set6: White balance: 3500–4000 K for natural greens.
post1.p.phone1: Modern phones (iPhone 12 and newer, Pixel 6+, Samsung S21+) handle Northern Lights photography surprisingly well in Night Mode. Two rules: keep the phone perfectly still on a small tripod or rest it on a wall, and let the exposure run its full length (often 10–30 seconds). Tap the darkest part of the sky to set focus.
post1.li.comp1: Include a foreground — a tree, cabin, frozen lake or person — to give the sky scale.
post1.li.comp2: Shoot wide enough to capture the arc but tight enough to avoid empty space.
post1.li.comp3: Reflections on water or wet ice double the drama.
post1.li.comp4: Avoid bright artificial lights in frame — they blow out instantly at high ISO.
post1.p.field1: Arrive before dark, find your composition while you can still see, and pre-focus on a distant light. Take a test shot, then leave the camera mostly alone — refocus only if you change focal length. Keep the lens hood on; frost is the enemy. If the front element fogs up, gently warm it with body heat, never breathe on it.
post1.p.safety1: Dress in layers, bring hand warmers, and tell someone where you are going. The best photos rarely happen in the parking lot — but never trade a shot for a dangerous detour onto unplowed roads or thin ice. Patience and warm boots win more Northern Lights nights than expensive gear.
post1.cta: Check the live forecast tonight — clear skies and Kp 3+ are usually all you need in Lapland.
blog.post2.title: Reading the Northern Lights forecast like a pro
blog.post2.excerpt: What Kp, Bz, solar wind and OVATION really mean — and how to combine them into a confident go/no-go decision.
post2.h1: Reading the Northern Lights forecast like a pro
post2.lead: Understanding Kp, Bz and solar wind makes Northern Lights forecasting much easier.
post2.p.kp1: Kp measures geomagnetic activity on a scale from 0 to 9. In Lapland even Kp 2–3 can produce visible Northern Lights.
post2.p.bz1: A negative Bz allows solar wind energy to enter Earth's magnetic field more efficiently, increasing Northern Lights activity.
post2.p.wind1: Fast solar wind often creates brighter and more active Northern Lights displays.
post2.p.combine1: Strong Northern Lights activity usually requires a combination of elevated Kp, strong solar wind and negative Bz.
post2.cta: Watch live solar data before heading outside.
blog.post3.title: Best months and hours for the Northern Lights
blog.post3.excerpt: When to chase the Northern Lights in Lapland — peak months, best hours of the night, moon phase and weather windows.
post3.h1: Best months and hours for the Northern Lights
post3.lead: Geomagnetic activity, darkness and weather all have to line up.
post3.p.season1: The best Northern Lights season in Lapland runs from late August until April.
post3.li.m1: September–October: dark skies return and geomagnetic activity increases.
post3.li.m2: February–March: long dark nights and often clearer skies.
post3.li.m3: December–January: longest nights but also more clouds.
post3.p.hours1: The best viewing hours are usually between 21:00 and 02:00.
post3.p.moon1: Clouds matter far more than moonlight. Clear skies are essential.
post3.p.cycle1: We are currently near solar maximum, which increases Northern Lights activity.
post3.cta: Pick a dark clear night and monitor the live Kp forecast.
